If I could teach one piece of grammar to everybody who negotiates in a second language, it would not be vocabulary and it would not be politeness formulas. It would be the second conditional. Here is why. In a negotiation you constantly need to find out what something is worth to the other side, and you cannot do that by offering it, because the moment you offer it you have given it away. So you say: if we accepted thirty days, what would you do about the fee? You have not accepted thirty days. Nothing has moved. But now you know what it is worth, and you can take the idea off the table without anybody losing anything. People who only have the first conditional negotiate in offers, and they run out of things to offer very quickly. People who have both can explore for an hour and commit in the last five minutes.

The strongest position in any negotiation is not being right. It is having somewhere else to go. If you have a genuine fallback, everything about the way you talk changes, and the other side hears it before you have said anything about it. You stop arguing and start explaining. You can say, honestly, that if we cannot agree on this we will do the other thing, and nobody hears a threat, because it is simply true. The mistake people make is bluffing. If you say you will walk away and you cannot, that gets found out in one meeting, and after that nothing you say has any weight at all. So my advice is to spend the week before a negotiation building the fallback rather than rehearsing the arguments. Arguments are cheap. Alternatives are what get you the clause.

Both sides open with the position they would like, and neither expects to get it. The sticking point is named out loud, so that the rest can stop being argued about. Ideas are explored in the second conditional, without anybody offering anything yet. One side gives ground on the term in exchange for holding firm on the fee. And what is left is either agreed on the call or escalated to somebody more senior.
